claim: Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are essential components of the ribosome and are among the most abundant macromolecules in the cell.
source: Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are essential components of the ribosome and are among the most abundant macromolecules in the cell.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about rRNAs.

claim: Eukaryotic genomes contain dozens to hundreds of rDNA genes.
source: To ensure high rRNA level, eukaryotic genomes contain dozens to hundreds of rDNA genes, however, only a fraction of the rRNA genes seems to be active, while others are transcriptionally silent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic genome organization.

claim: Only a fraction of rRNA genes are active, while others are transcriptionally silent.
source: To ensure high rRNA level, eukaryotic genomes contain dozens to hundreds of rDNA genes, however, only a fraction of the rRNA genes seems to be active, while others are transcriptionally silent.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Individual rDNA genes have high level of cell-to-cell heterogeneity in their expression in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: We found that individual rDNA genes have high level of cell-to-cell heterogeneity in their expression in Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Insertion of heterologous sequences into rDNA leads to repression associated with reduced expression in individual cells and decreased number of cells expressing rDNA with insertions.
source: Insertion of heterologous sequences into rDNA leads to repression associated with reduced expression in individual cells and decreased number of cells expressing rDNA with insertions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR and HCR-FISH data in Figure 2.

claim: SUMO (Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier) and SUMO ligase Ubc9 are required for efficient repression of interrupted rDNA units.
source: We found that SUMO (Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier) and SUMO ligase Ubc9 are required for efficient repression of interrupted rDNA units and variable expression of intact rDNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: SUMO and SUMO ligase Ubc9 are required for variable expression of intact rDNA.
source: We found that SUMO (Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier) and SUMO ligase Ubc9 are required for efficient repression of interrupted rDNA units and variable expression of intact rDNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Disruption of the SUMO pathway abolishes discrimination of interrupted and intact rDNAs.
source: Disruption of the SUMO pathway abolishes discrimination of interrupted and intact rDNAs and removes cell-to-cell heterogeneity leading to uniformly high expression of individual rDNA in single cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4 showing similar expression levels of intact and interrupted rDNA upon SUMO knockdown.

claim: Disruption of the SUMO pathway removes cell-to-cell heterogeneity leading to uniformly high expression of individual rDNA in single cells.
source: Disruption of the SUMO pathway abolishes discrimination of interrupted and intact rDNAs and removes cell-to-cell heterogeneity leading to uniformly high expression of individual rDNA in single cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data in Figure 4C showing expression in all nuclei upon SUMO knockdown.

claim: The SUMO pathway is responsible for both repression of interrupted units and control of intact rDNA expression.
source: Our results suggest that the SUMO pathway is responsible for both repression of interrupted units and control of intact rDNA expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing SUMO effects on both intact and interrupted rDNA.

claim: rRNA genes encoding the 18S, 28S, and 5.8S rRNAs are transcribed under the control of a single promoter producing pre-rRNA in most eukaryotes.
source: In most eukaryotes rRNA genes encoding the 18S, 28S, and 5.8S rRNAs are transcribed under the control of a single promoter producing pre-rRNA (Mandal, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Mandal, 1984.

claim: Pre-rRNA is converted to mature 18S, 28S, and 5.8S rRNAs after co-transcriptional processing and modification.
source: After co-transcriptional processing and modification, the pre-RNA is converted to mature 18S, 28S, and 5.8S rRNAs, which together with the additional 5S rRNA and ribosomal proteins are assembled into pre-ribosomal subunits (Henras et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Henras et al., 2015.

claim: Actively transcribed rDNA genes and pre-ribosomal subunits at different steps of maturity form the nucleolus.
source: Actively transcribed rDNA genes and pre-ribosomal subunits at different steps of maturity form the nucleolus – a membraneless compartment in the nucleus characterized by tripartite morphological ultrastructure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleolus structure and function.

claim: The nucleolus is a membraneless compartment in the nucleus characterized by tripartite morphological ultrastructure.
source: Actively transcribed rDNA genes and pre-ribosomal subunits at different steps of maturity form the nucleolus – a membraneless compartment in the nucleus characterized by tripartite morphological ultrastructure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleolus structure.

claim: In eukaryotic genomes dozens to hundreds of nearly identical rDNA units are arranged head-to-tail forming one or several clusters.
source: In eukaryotic genomes dozens to hundreds of nearly identical rDNA units are arranged head-to-tail forming one or several clusters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rDNA organization.

claim: Only a fraction of available rDNA genes is transcriptionally active in diverse organisms including plants, yeast, fruit flies, mice and humans.
source: Studies in such diverse organisms as different plants, yeast, fruit flies, mice and humans showed that only fraction of available rDNA genes is transcriptionally active (Bird et al., 1981; Coffman et al., 2005; Conconi et al., 1989; Dammann et al., 1993; Flavell et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In organisms with several rDNA clusters on different chromosomes, whole clusters might be transcriptionally inactive and positioned outside of the nucleolus.
source: In organisms that have several rDNA clusters located on different chromosomes, whole clusters might be transcriptionally inactive and positioned outside of the nucleolus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rDNA cluster regulation.

claim: In Drosophila where rDNA clusters are located on the X and Y chromosomes, in certain genotypes only the Y chromosome cluster is active and forms the nucleolus.
source: For example, in Drosophila where rDNA clusters are located on the X and Y chromosomes, in certain genotypes only the Y chromosome cluster is active and forms the nucleolus (Greil and Ahmad, 2012; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Greil and Ahmad, 2012 and Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: In mammals, some ribosomal loci clusters are constantly active, while the activity of others depends on tissue type, presence of nutrients and stress.
source: In mammals which carry several ribosomal loci on different chromosomes some clusters are constantly active, while the activity of others depends on the tissue type, presence of nutrients and stress (Ali et al., 2008; Ali et al., 2012; de Capoa et al., 1985a; de Capoa et al., 1985b; Tseng et al., 2008; Young et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Individual rDNA units within a single cluster have different transcriptional activity and are subject to all-or-none regulation.
source: Direct observation of rDNA transcription by electron microscopy showed that individual rDNA units within a single cluster might also have different transcriptional activity and are subject to all-or-none regulation: any given rDNA unit is either actively transcribed with multiple RNA pol I associated with nascent pre-rRNA positioned along the body of the unit, or is inactive. (Foe, 1978; McKnight and Miller, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Any given rDNA unit is either actively transcribed with multiple RNA pol I associated with nascent pre-rRNA positioned along the body of the unit, or is inactive.
source: Direct observation of rDNA transcription by electron microscopy showed that individual rDNA units within a single cluster might also have different transcriptional activity and are subject to all-or-none regulation: any given rDNA unit is either actively transcribed with multiple RNA pol I associated with nascent pre-rRNA positioned along the body of the unit, or is inactive. (Foe, 1978; McKnight and Miller, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Individual rDNA units are similar in sequence due to recombination-driven homogenization.
source: Due to recombination-driven homogenization, individual rDNA units are similar in sequence (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2007), arguing against difference in sequence leading to differential expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Eickbush and Eickbush, 2007.

claim: Repressed rDNA units might become active when the genetic environment or demand for rRNA production changes.
source: In fact, repressed rDNA units might become active when the genetic environment or demand for rRNA production changes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rDNA regulation.

claim: In Drosophila X-linked rDNA genes that are inactive in males are active in females.
source: For example, in Drosophila X-linked rDNA genes that are inactive in males are active in females (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: In mammals repressed rDNA units are enriched in DNA methylation and repressive histone marks.
source: In mammals repressed rDNA units are enriched in DNA methylation, repressive histone marks (Coffman et al., 2005; Earley et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006; Santoro and Grummt, 2001; Santoro et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The chromatin remodeling complexes NoRC and NuRD, in cooperation with noncoding RNAs derived from rDNA loci, are involved in rDNA repression.
source: The chromatin remodeling complexes NoRC and NuRD, in cooperation with noncoding RNAs derived from rDNA loci were shown to be involved in rDNA repression (Santoro et al., 2002; Strohner et al., 2001; Xie et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2002; Bierhoff et al., 2014; Mayer et al., 2006; Santoro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A deep understanding of the molecular mechanisms establishing and maintaining rDNA repression is lacking.
source: However, a deep understanding of the molecular mechanisms establishing and maintaining rDNA repression is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Genomes of many arthropod species including Drosophila melanogaster harbor transposable elements that integrate into rDNA, creating distinct rDNA units.
source: Genomes of many arthropod species including Drosophila melanogaster harbor transposable elements that integrate into rDNA, creating distinct rDNA units.
evidence: This is established knowledge about arthropod genomes.

claim: R1 and R2 belong to the non-long terminal repeat (non-LTR) retrotransposons and encode a sequence-specific endonuclease that is responsible for integration of these elements into 28S rDNA.
source: R1 and R2 belong to the non-long terminal repeat (non-LTR) retrotransposons and encode a sequence-specific endonuclease that is responsible for integration of these elements into 28S rDNA (Burke et al., 1987; Eickbush and Eickbush, 2015; Jakubczak et al., 1990; Xiong et al., 1988; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: R1 and R2 lack their own promoters and instead rely on the rDNA transcription machinery for their expression by transcribing as part of pre-rRNA followed by excision mediated by the transposon-encoded ribozyme.
source: It is believed that R1 and R2 lack their own promoters and instead rely on the rDNA transcription machinery for their expression by transcribing as part of pre-rRNA followed by excision mediated by the transposon-encoded ribozyme (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2010; Eickbush et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The fraction of rDNA units with R1 and R2 insertions varies between different D. melanogaster strains, but was estimated to reach up to 80% of units in some strains.
source: The fraction of rDNA units with R1 and R2 insertions varies between different D. melanogaster strains, but was estimated to reach up to 80% of units in some strains (Jakubczak et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jakubczak et al., 1992.

claim: Despite the abundance of R1 and R2, their expression level is usually low.
source: Despite the abundance of R1 and R2, their expression level is usually low.
evidence: This is established knowledge about R1 and R2 expression.

claim: Electron microscopy and run-on analysis of nascent transcripts revealed that rDNA units with transposon insertions are transcriptionally silent.
source: Indeed, electron microscopy and run-on analysis of nascent transcripts revealed that rDNA units with transposon insertions are transcriptionally silent, indicating a mechanism that can distinguish interrupted rDNA copies and repress their transcription (Jamrich and Miller, 1984; Ye and Eickbush, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Jamrich and Miller, 1984 and Ye and Eickbush, 2006.

claim: R1 and R2 expression is increased if the total number of rDNA units in the genome is low.
source: Interestingly, R1 and R2 expression is increased if the total number of rDNA units in the genome is low, suggesting that repression is sensitive to cellular rRNA demand (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003; Long et al., 1981; Terracol, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Repression of interrupted rDNA is sensitive to cellular rRNA demand.
source: Interestingly, R1 and R2 expression is increased if the total number of rDNA units in the genome is low, suggesting that repression is sensitive to cellular rRNA demand (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003; Long et al., 1981; Terracol, 1986).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that R1 and R2 expression increases when rDNA copy number is low.

claim: The molecular mechanism for repression of interrupted rDNA units and its relationship to the general mechanism of rDNA silencing remained unknown.
source: The molecular mechanism for repression of interrupted rDNA units and its relationship to the general mechanism of rDNA silencing remained unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: SUMO (Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier) is a small protein related to ubiquitin that is covalently attached to other proteins in sequential reactions mediated by E1, E2 and, for some targets, E3 SUMO ligases.
source: SUMO (Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier) is a small protein related to ubiquitin that is covalently attached to other proteins in sequential reactions mediated by E1, E2 and, for some targets, E3 SUMO ligases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO biochemistry.

claim: Unlike ubiquitination, SUMOylation typically is not linked to protein degradation and instead changes protein-protein interactions.
source: Unlike ubiquitination, SUMOylation typically is not linked to protein degradation and instead changes protein-protein interactions by facilitating recruitment of new binding partners or masking existing binding sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO function.

claim: The majority of SUMOylated proteins reside in the nucleus.
source: The majority of SUMOylated proteins reside in the nucleus and SUMOylation was shown to be involved in regulation of transcription, mRNA processing, chromatin organization, replication and repair (Geiss-Friedlander and Melchior, 2007) as well as rRNA maturation and nucleolus function (Finkbeiner et al., 2011; Haindl et al., 2008; Yun et al., 2008; Westman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SUMOylation is involved in regulation of transcription, mRNA processing, chromatin organization, replication and repair.
source: The majority of SUMOylated proteins reside in the nucleus and SUMOylation was shown to be involved in regulation of transcription, mRNA processing, chromatin organization, replication and repair (Geiss-Friedlander and Melchior, 2007) as well as rRNA maturation and nucleolus function (Finkbeiner et al., 2011; Haindl et al., 2008; Yun et al., 2008; Westman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Geiss-Friedlander and Melchior, 2007.

claim: SUMOylation is involved in rRNA maturation and nucleolus function.
source: The majority of SUMOylated proteins reside in the nucleus and SUMOylation was shown to be involved in regulation of transcription, mRNA processing, chromatin organization, replication and repair (Geiss-Friedlander and Melchior, 2007) as well as rRNA maturation and nucleolus function (Finkbeiner et al., 2011; Haindl et al., 2008; Yun et al., 2008; Westman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SUMOylation is essential for growth and viability of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: SUMOylation was shown to be essential for growth and viability of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Johnson et al., 1997), D. melanogaster (Lehembre et al., 2000) and mice (Nacerddine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Johnson et al., 1997.

claim: SUMOylation is essential for growth and viability of D. melanogaster.
source: SUMOylation was shown to be essential for growth and viability of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Johnson et al., 1997), D. melanogaster (Lehembre et al., 2000) and mice (Nacerddine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lehembre et al., 2000.

claim: SUMOylation is essential for growth and viability of mice.
source: SUMOylation was shown to be essential for growth and viability of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Johnson et al., 1997), D. melanogaster (Lehembre et al., 2000) and mice (Nacerddine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Nacerddine et al., 2005.

claim: Mammalian genomes encode four distinct SUMO genes with partially redundant functions.
source: Mammalian genomes encode four distinct SUMO genes with partially redundant functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian SUMO genes.

claim: Only one SUMO gene is present in the D. melanogaster genome.
source: In contrast, only one SUMO gene is present in the D. melanogaster genome, making it a good model to understand the diverse functions of SUMOylation (Guo et al., 2004; Melchior, 2000; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: D. melanogaster is a good model to understand the diverse functions of SUMOylation due to having only one SUMO gene.
source: In contrast, only one SUMO gene is present in the D. melanogaster genome, making it a good model to understand the diverse functions of SUMOylation (Guo et al., 2004; Melchior, 2000; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that having a single SUMO gene simplifies genetic analysis.

claim: The D. melanogaster genome contains numerous (50-200) rDNA units arranged in tandem repeats in the heterochromatin of the X and Y chromosomes.
source: The D. melanogaster genome contain numerous (50-200) rDNA units arranged in tandem repeats in the heterochromatin of the X and Y chromosomes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila genome organization, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Many rDNA units contain insertions of R1 and R2 transposons that lack their own promoters and co-transcribe with pre-rRNA.
source: Many rDNA units contain insertions of R1 and R2 transposons that lack their own promoters and co-transcribe with pre-rRNA (Ye and Eickbush, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ye and Eickbush, 2006.

claim: Expression of R1 and R2 elements is low in the majority of Drosophila strains, indicating that units with insertions are specifically repressed.
source: However, expression of R1 and R2 elements is low in the majority of Drosophila strains, indicating that units with insertions are specifically repressed (Ye and Eickbush, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ye and Eickbush, 2006.

claim: The large number of identical rDNA units organized in large arrays makes it impossible to study expression of individual rDNA units by conventional methods.
source: The large number of identical rDNA units organized in large arrays makes it impossible to study expression of individual rDNA units by conventional methods.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations in studying rDNA.

claim: The rDNA transgene harbors the non-transcribed spacer (NTS), which includes elements that regulate RNA polymerase I (Pol I) transcription and the complete transcribed portion, which generates the 47S pre-rRNA.
source: It harbors the non-transcribed spacer (NTS), which includes elements that regulate RNA polymerase I (Pol I) transcription and the complete transcribed portion, which generates the 47S pre-rRNA.
evidence: This describes the structure of the transgene construct used in the study.

claim: A 21 bp unique identification sequence (UID) was inserted into the external transcribed spacer (ETS) downstream of the transcription start site to discriminate transgene transcripts from endogenous rRNA.
source: To discriminate transcripts generated from the transgene from endogenous rRNA we inserted a 21 bp unique identification sequence (UID) into the external transcribed spacer (ETS) downstream of the transcription start site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the transgene construct.

claim: The UID sequence is removed from pre-rRNA during its processing to mature rRNAs in the nucleolus.
source: Along with the rest of the ETS, the UID sequence is removed from pre-rRNA during its processing to mature rRNAs in the nucleolus, however, it allowed us to monitor transgene transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of rRNA processing and the location of the UID in the ETS.

claim: The single-unit rDNA transgene was integrated into a euchromatic site on 2nd chromosome (chr 2L: 1,582,820) using site-specific integration.
source: In contrast to endogenous rDNA arrays, which are located in heterochromatin of the X and Y chromosomes, the single-unit rDNA transgene was integrated into a euchromatic site on 2nd chromosome (chr 2L: 1,582,820) using site-specific integration.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and genomic location of the transgene.

claim: RT-qPCR with one primer specific to UID sequence detected expression of the rDNA transgene in transgenic flies.
source: RT-qPCR with one primer specific to UID sequence detected expression of the rDNA transgene in transgenic flies, while no PCR product was produced in the parental strain used for transgenesis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No PCR product was produced in the parental strain used for transgenesis when using UID-specific primers.
source: RT-qPCR with one primer specific to UID sequence detected expression of the rDNA transgene in transgenic flies, while no PCR product was produced in the parental strain used for transgenesis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 1B demonstrating specificity of the UID detection.

claim: RT-qPCR is able to discriminate expression of the marked rDNA transgene from endogenous rDNA.
source: Thus, RT-qPCR is able to discriminate expression of the marked rDNA transgene from endogenous rDNA and insertion of UID sequence does not disrupt the Pol I promoter and enhancer elements.
evidence: This is concluded from the RT-qPCR results showing specific detection of transgene expression.

claim: Insertion of UID sequence does not disrupt the Pol I promoter and enhancer elements.
source: Thus, RT-qPCR is able to discriminate expression of the marked rDNA transgene from endogenous rDNA and insertion of UID sequence does not disrupt the Pol I promoter and enhancer elements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the transgene is expressed.

claim: HCR-FISH allowed specific detection of nascent transgene transcripts.
source: HCR-FISH allowed specific detection of nascent transgene transcripts and revealed that transgene RNA is present exclusively in the nucleus (Figure 1C) consistent with the ETS portion being processed out of pre-rRNA and degraded soon after transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Transgene RNA is present exclusively in the nucleus.
source: HCR-FISH allowed specific detection of nascent transgene transcripts and revealed that transgene RNA is present exclusively in the nucleus (Figure 1C) consistent with the ETS portion being processed out of pre-rRNA and degraded soon after transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ETS portion is processed out of pre-rRNA and degraded soon after transcription.
source: HCR-FISH allowed specific detection of nascent transgene transcripts and revealed that transgene RNA is present exclusively in the nucleus (Figure 1C) consistent with the ETS portion being processed out of pre-rRNA and degraded soon after transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the nuclear localization of transgene RNA and knowledge of rRNA processing.

claim: The marked rDNA transgene enables expression analysis of an individual rDNA unit inserted in a heterologous genomic location.
source: Thus, the marked rDNA transgene enables expression analysis of an individual rDNA unit inserted in a heterologous genomic location.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the successful detection of transgene expression.

claim: In Drosophila significant fraction of rDNA units contain insertions of R1 and R2 retrotransposons.
source: In Drosophila significant fraction of rDNA units contain insertions of R1 and R2 retrotransposons, however, units interrupted by transposon insertions are usually silent (Long and Dawid, 1979; Jamrich and Miller, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Units interrupted by transposon insertions are usually silent.
source: In Drosophila significant fraction of rDNA units contain insertions of R1 and R2 retrotransposons, however, units interrupted by transposon insertions are usually silent (Long and Dawid, 1979; Jamrich and Miller, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: R1 integrates into 28S rDNA at position 2711 nt.
source: R1 and R2 each integrate into single unique site positioned in 28S RNA at 2711 nt and 2648 nt of 28S (Jakubczak et al., 1990), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jakubczak et al., 1990.

claim: R2 integrates into 28S rDNA at position 2648 nt.
source: R1 and R2 each integrate into single unique site positioned in 28S RNA at 2711 nt and 2648 nt of 28S (Jakubczak et al., 1990), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jakubczak et al., 1990.

claim: The full-length R1 is 5.3 Kb.
source: The full-length R1 (5.3 Kb) and R2 (3.6 Kb) transposon sequences were inserted in their respective integration sites within the 28S rDNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the transgene constructs used in the study.

claim: The full-length R2 is 3.6 Kb.
source: The full-length R1 (5.3 Kb) and R2 (3.6 Kb) transposon sequences were inserted in their respective integration sites within the 28S rDNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the transgene constructs used in the study.

claim: All transgenes were integrated into the same genomic location.
source: All transgenes were integrated into the same genomic location, which allows us to directly compare their expression.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for position effects.

claim: Transposon insertions lead to a 3- to 5-fold reduction in pre-rRNA level compared to the intact transgene.
source: Expression analysis of transgenes by RT-qPCR in ovary and carcass (Figure 2B) showed that transposon insertions lead to a 3- to 5-fold reduction in pre-rRNA level compared to the intact transgene.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: R1 insertion caused a slightly stronger reduction in expression compared to R2 insertion.
source: R1 insertion caused a slightly stronger reduction in expression compared to R2 insertion.
evidence: This is observed from the RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Insertions of a non-transposon CFP sequence lead to comparable decrease in expression.
source: Importantly, insertions of a non-transposon CFP sequence lead to comparable decrease in expression, indicating that the repressive effect is not dependent on a specific transposon sequence and can be triggered by heterologous sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: The repressive effect is not dependent on a specific transposon sequence and can be triggered by heterologous sequence.
source: Importantly, insertions of a non-transposon CFP sequence lead to comparable decrease in expression, indicating that the repressive effect is not dependent on a specific transposon sequence and can be triggered by heterologous sequence.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that CFP insertion causes similar repression as transposon insertions.

claim: A 29 bp insertion caused a 2-fold decrease in transgene expression.
source: A 29 bp insertion caused a 2-fold decrease in transgene expression, demonstrating that short insertions can affect rDNA expression, though to a lesser degree.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Short insertions can affect rDNA expression, though to a lesser degree than longer insertions.
source: A 29 bp insertion caused a 2-fold decrease in transgene expression, demonstrating that short insertions can affect rDNA expression, though to a lesser degree.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the effect of 29 bp insertion to longer insertions.

claim: Expression of the single-copy rDNA transgene recapitulates the behavior of endogenous rDNA and demonstrates repression of units interrupted by transposon insertions.
source: Thus, expression of the single-copy rDNA transgene recapitulates the behavior of endogenous rDNA and demonstrates repression of units interrupted by transposon insertions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the transgene expression data showing repression upon insertion.

claim: Nurse cells of the fly ovary are an ideal cell type to study transgene expression as each egg chamber is composed of 15 identical sister nurse cells with large nuclei.
source: Nurse cells of the fly ovary are an ideal cell type to study transgene expression as each egg chamber is composed of 15 identical sister nurse cells with large nuclei.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system used in the study.

claim: The chromosomes of nurse cells forming one egg chamber undergo several rounds of endoreplication.
source: The chromosomes of nurse cells forming one egg chamber undergo several rounds of endoreplication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nurse cell biology.

claim: Due to chromosome polytenization the HCR-FISH signals of rDNA transgenes and the endogenous control gene, vasa, are localized to several distinct loci on chromatin that likely represent sites of nascent transcription.
source: Due to chromosome polytenization the HCR-FISH signals of rDNA transgenes and the endogenous control gene, vasa, are localized to several distinct loci on chromatin that likely represent sites of nascent transcription (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed from HCR-FISH data in Figure 2C and inferred from knowledge of polytene chromosomes.

claim: Vasa gene was expressed at similar levels in 15 nurse cells forming egg chamber.
source: Vasa gene was expressed at similar levels in 15 nurse cells forming egg chamber.
evidence: This is observed from HCR-FISH data in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of endogenous pre-rRNA detected by FISH probe against ETS was similar in the different nuclei.
source: Expression of endogenous pre-rRNA detected by FISH probe against ETS (which detects rRNAs coming from all rDNA copies) was also similar in the different nuclei.
evidence: This is observed from HCR-FISH data in Figure 2C.

claim: The rDNA transgenes have variable levels of expression in individual nuclei within one egg chamber with some nuclei showing no signal at all, while others had variable signal intensity.
source: In contrast, the rDNA transgenes have variable levels of expression in individual nuclei within one egg chamber with some nuclei showing no signal at all, while others had variable signal intensity.
evidence: This is a primary finding observed from HCR-FISH data in Figure 2C.

claim: Nascent transgenic transcripts often co-localize with endogenous pre-rRNA.
source: Double FISH demonstrated that nascent transgenic transcripts often co-localize with endogenous pre-rRNA (Figure 2C) indicating that transgene locus is recruited to nucleolus.
evidence: This is observed from double FISH data in Figure 2C.

claim: Transgene locus is recruited to nucleolus.
source: Double FISH demonstrated that nascent transgenic transcripts often co-localize with endogenous pre-rRNA (Figure 2C) indicating that transgene locus is recruited to nucleolus.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of transgene transcripts with endogenous pre-rRNA.

claim: The intact rDNA transgene is expressed in the majority (10 ± 1 out 15, 67%), but not all cells of the egg chamber.
source: The intact rDNA transgene is expressed in the majority (10 ± 1 out 15, 67%), but not all cells of the egg chamber (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The fraction of individual nuclei with detectable FISH signal drops to 27% for transgenes with R1 and R2 insertions.
source: The fraction of individual nuclei with detectable FISH signal drops to 27% for transgenes with R1 and R2 insertions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The intact rDNA transgene showed high level of cell-to-cell variability in expression.
source: The intact rDNA transgene showed high level of cell-to-cell variability in expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH signal intensity data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The signal intensity was ~30 fold lower for transgenes containing R1 and R2 insertions compared to intact rDNA transgene.

claim: R1 and R2 become among the top 20 most abundant cellular mRNA upon smt3 GLKD.
source: RNA-seq analysis showed that the levels of R1 and R2 transcripts increased ~1000 and~300 fold, respectively, and they become among the top 20 most abundant cellular mRNA (an average of 3164 and 3421 TPM (transcripts per million) in smt3 GLKD, compared to 2.76 and 10.84 TPMs in control ovaries) (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The extremely strong R1 and R2 activation upon depletion of SUMO was confirmed by RT-qPCR.
source: The extremely strong R1 and R2 activation upon depletion of SUMO was also confirmed by RT-qPCR (Figure 3D).

claim: The vast majority of other transposons and genes whose expression was affected by smt3 GLKD changed less than 10-fold.
source: Analysis of RNA-seq data demonstrated that such strong up-regulation is exclusive for R1 and R2 and is not seen for any other protein-coding or ncRNA genes: the vast majority of other transposons and genes those expression was affected by smt3 GLKD changed less than 10-fold.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SUMO seems to be involved in specific process of R1/R2 repression.
source: Thus, SUMO seems to be involved in specific process of R1/R2 repression.

claim: RT-qPCR showed strong and specific upregulation of R1 and R2 upon both smt3 and Ubc9 knock-downs in S2 cells.
source: RT-qPCR showed strong and specific upregulation of R1 and R2 upon both smt3 and Ubc9 knock-downs in S2 cells (Figure 3E).

source: Thus, SUMO is required for the potent and specific repression of R1 and R2 in both the soma and the germline, employing a mechanism that is independent of piRNA.

claim: R1 and R2 are embedded into rDNA and use the rRNA transcription machinery for their expression.
source: R1 and R2 are embedded into rDNA and use the rRNA transcription machinery for their expression suggesting that SUMO controls expression of rDNA units interrupted by transposon insertions.

source: R1 and R2 are embedded into rDNA and use the rRNA transcription machinery for their expression suggesting that SUMO controls expression of rDNA units interrupted by transposon insertions.

source: Transgenes with R1 and R2 insertions showed 54-fold and 50-fold increase in pre-rRNA expression level upon Smt3 KD (Figure 4A).

source: Different transgenes with R1 and R2 as well as CFP insertions showed similar 41- to 54-fold increase in pre-rRNA level.

source: Thus, the function of SUMO in repression of endogenous rDNA units with insertion of R1 and R2 transposons is recapitulated using rDNA transgenes.
evidence: This is concluded from the similar effects of SUMO depletion on endogenous and transgenic rDNA.

claim: Expression of the intact rDNA transgene that lacks any insertion was up-regulated ~12 fold upon SUMO KD.
source: Surprisingly, expression of the intact rDNA transgene that lacks any insertion was also up-regulated ~12 fold upon SUMO KD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In wild-type flies interrupted rDNA copies are repressed compared to intact units.
source: While in wild-type flies interrupted rDNA copies are repressed compared to intact units (Figure 2), intact and interrupted copies have similar expression levels in the absence of SUMO.
evidence: This is observed from comparing expression data in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Intact and interrupted copies have similar expression levels in the absence of SUMO.
source: While in wild-type flies interrupted rDNA copies are repressed compared to intact units (Figure 2), intact and interrupted copies have similar expression levels in the absence of SUMO.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SUMO is required for differential expression of intact and interrupted rDNA.
source: Thus, SUMO is required for differential expression of intact and interrupted rDNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that SUMO depletion equalizes expression of intact and interrupted rDNA.

claim: SUMO pathway participates in repression of both intact and interrupted rRNA, but does so with different efficiency.
source: SUMO pathway participates in repression of both intact and interrupted rRNA, but does so with different efficiency.
evidence: This is concluded from the different fold-changes in expression upon SUMO depletion for intact vs interrupted rDNA.

claim: Smt3 GLKD lead to a marked increase in expression of both intact and interrupted rDNA transgenes as detected by HCR-FISH.
source: Confirming the RT-qPCR results, Smt3 GLKD lead to a marked increase in expression of both intact and interrupted rDNA transgenes.

source: Second, depletion of SUMO increased the signal intensity per nucleus: after Smt3 KD the signal increased 35 ~ 37 fold for interrupted transgenes and ~2.5 fold for the intact transgene (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH signal intensity data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Intact and interrupted transgenes showed similarly high expression level upon SUMO KD.
source: Consistent with the RT-qPCR results, intact and interrupted transgenes showed similarly high expression level upon SUMO KD.

claim: While interrupted units are preferentially silenced in wild-type cells, loss of SUMO eliminates differential repression.
source: Thus, while interrupted units are preferentially silenced in wild-type cells, loss of SUMO eliminates differential repression.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing expression of intact and interrupted rDNA in wild-type and SUMO-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of Smt3 led to 2.5-fold increase in pre-rRNA levels both in ovarian germ cells and in S2 cells.
source: Depletion of Smt3 led to 2.5-fold increase in pre-rRNA levels both in ovarian germ cells and in S2 cells (Figure 4E), demonstrating that SUMO controls expression of endogenous rDNA arrays.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SUMO controls expression of endogenous rDNA arrays.
source: Depletion of Smt3 led to 2.5-fold increase in pre-rRNA levels both in ovarian germ cells and in S2 cells (Figure 4E), demonstrating that SUMO controls expression of endogenous rDNA arrays.
evidence: This is concluded from the increase in pre-rRNA levels upon SUMO depletion.

claim: GFP-tagged Rpl135 localized to the nucleolus.

source: Rpl135 ChIP-qPCR using a GFP antibody showed enrichment of Pol I on the ETS portion and on 18S of native rDNA units (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Enrichment of Pol I was detected on promoters of the rDNA transgenes.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: The SUMO-dependent pathway regulates rDNA transcription.
source: Importantly, depletion of SUMO caused 2.5 to 4-fold increase in the levels of Pol I on intact and interrupted transgenes (Figure 5A), indicating that the SUMO-dependent pathway regulates rDNA transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the increased Pol I occupancy upon SUMO depletion.

claim: H3K9me3 was proposed to play a role in rDNA silencing.
source: H3K9me3 was proposed to play a role in rDNA silencing (Santoro et al., 2002).

claim: No change in H3K9me3 occupancy was observed upon SUMO depletion on endogenous rDNA units and R1 and R2 sequences.
source: We found that endogenous rDNA units and R1 and R2 sequences are indeed enriched in H3K9me3 mark in wild-type flies, however, no change in H3K9me3 occupancy was observed upon SUMO depletion (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: R1 and R2 sequences are heterochromatic.
source: These experiments confirmed that R1 and R2 sequences are heterochromatic.

source: Taken together, these results indicate that the levels of H3K9me3 mark on endogenous and transgenic rDNA do not show clear correlation with silencing.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP data showing no change in H3K9me3 upon SUMO depletion despite increased expression.

claim: SetDB1, Su(var)3–9 and G9a are together responsible for all mono-, di- and trimethylation of H3K9 in Drosophila.
source: To further explore the role of heterochromatin marks in repression of rDNA we used RNAi to knock-down three histone methyltransferases, SetDB1, Su(var)3–9 and G9a, that are together responsible for all mono-, di- and trimethylation of H3K9 in Drosophila (Supplementary file 4).

claim: Depletion of SetDB1 and G9a had no effect on R1 and R2 expression.

claim: Depletion of Su(var)3–9 caused ~2.5 fold change in R1 and R2 expression.
source: Depletion of SetDB1 and G9a had no effect on R1 and R2 expression, while depletion of Su(var)3–9 caused ~2.5 fold change (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of all three histone methyltransferases had the similar effect as depletion of Su(var)3–9 alone indicating no redundancy.
source: Simultaneous knockdown of all three histone methyltransferases had the similar effect as depletion of Su(var)3–9 alone indicating no redundancy.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

source: Thus, knock-down of H3K9 methyltransferases induces mild derepression of R1 and R2 compared to strong upregulation upon smt3 and Ubc9 RNAi.

claim: Proteomic studies in Drosophila identified several hundred SUMOylated proteins.

evidence: This is inferred from knowledge about SUMOylation and technical limitations.

claim: rDNA repression might be caused by SUMOylation of chromatin proteins on rDNA sequences.
source: Many chromatin proteins, including histones, are substrates of SUMOylation (Shiio and Eisenman, 2003; Nathan et al., 2003) suggesting a possibility that rDNA repression might be caused by SUMOylation of chromatin proteins on rDNA sequences.
evidence: This is speculation based on known SUMOylation of chromatin proteins.

source: This analysis revealed enrichment of SUMO at rDNA unit and R2 sequences as well as at the 5' regions of the R1 transposon (Figure 6A) indicating that SUMOylated proteins are indeed enriched on rDNA chromatin.

claim: SUMOylated proteins are enriched on rDNA chromatin.
source: This analysis revealed enrichment of SUMO at rDNA unit and R2 sequences as well as at the 5' regions of the R1 transposon (Figure 6A) indicating that SUMOylated proteins are indeed enriched on rDNA chromatin.
evidence: This is concluded from the SUMO ChIP-seq data.

claim: SUMOylation was detected for Udd and CG3756, two proteins involved in RNA pol I dependent transcription of rDNA.
source: Out of 7 other candidates we detected SUMOylation of three proteins including Udd and CG3756, two proteins involved in RNA pol I dependent transcription of rDNA (Figure 6B).

source: This analysis showed that 77% of nucleolar genes have products harboring a SUMOylation consensus.

source: In addition, 68% (19 out of 28) genes associated with the biological process 'transcription by RNA polymerase I' (GO:0006360) have a SUMOylation consensus.
evidence: This is a finding from computational analysis of Pol I-related protein sequences.

source: Ontology analysis revealed that 27 out of 823 SUMOylated proteins are associated with the GO term 'nucleolus' demonstrating significant enrichment of nucleolar proteins among SUMOylated proteins (BH = adjusted p-value<0.01) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Many proteins involved in nucleolar function and rDNA transcription are SUMOylated.
source: Taken together, the results of experimental and computational analyses indicate that many proteins involved in nucleolar function and rDNA transcription are SUMOylated.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental SUMOylation assays and computational analyses.

claim: Knockdown of five genes (Ulp1, CG13773 CG3756, Fib, mbm) caused increase in expression of R1 and R2.
source: Out of 25 tested genes, knockdown of five (Ulp1, CG13773 CG3756, Fib, mbm) caused increase in expression of R1 and R2, including SUMO isopeptidase Ulp1 (Figure 6C).

source: None of tested E3 SUMO ligases scored positive.

evidence: This is observed from comparing the RNAi screen results to SUMO knockdown effects.

claim: Multiple proteins including several SUMOylated components of RNA pol I complex are involved in SUMO-dependent rDNA regulation.
source: Overall, the results of RNAi screen further support the role of SUMO pathway in rDNA regulation and suggest that multiple proteins including several SUMOylated components of RNA pol I complex are involved in this process.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNAi screen results.

claim: Expression of Ubc9 fused to Csy4 lead to 4.7-fold decrease in transgene expression compared to control flies.
source: Expression of Ubc9 fused to Csy4 lead to 4.7-fold decrease in transgene expression compared to control flies suggesting that increase in local SUMOylation lead to further rDNA repression (Figure 6D).

claim: Increase in local SUMOylation leads to further rDNA repression.
source: Expression of Ubc9 fused to Csy4 lead to 4.7-fold decrease in transgene expression compared to control flies suggesting that increase in local SUMOylation lead to further rDNA repression (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is concluded from the tethering experiment results.

claim: Studies in many eukaryotic species demonstrated that only a fraction of available rDNA genes are expressed, while other rDNA units with apparently identical sequence are inactive.
source: However, studies in many eukaryotic species paradoxically demonstrated that only a fraction of available rDNA genes are expressed, while other rDNA units with apparently identical sequence are inactive (Conconi et al., 1989; Morgan et al., 1983; Sogo et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: rDNA repression was linked to rDNA stability, prevention of recombination and preserving nucleolar structure.
source: rDNA repression was linked to rDNA stability, prevention of recombination and preserving nucleolar structure (Espada et al., 2007; Sinclair et al., 1997; Oakes et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Differential expression of ribosomal RNA genes represents an ultimate case of epigenetic regulation.
source: Differential expression of ribosomal RNA genes represents an ultimate case of epigenetic regulation: identical DNA sequences have drastically different expression levels within a single cell and these expression states are propagated through multiple cellular divisions.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of rDNA regulation.

claim: Hundreds of rDNA units are present in the genome with almost identical sequence, which cannot be reliably discriminated.
source: Studies of rDNA repression are hampered by the fact that hundreds of rDNA units are present in the genome with almost identical sequence, which cannot be reliably discriminated (Ganley and Kobayashi, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges in studying rDNA, supported by citation.

claim: Individual ribosomal RNA units inserted in a heterologous genomic position outside of the native rDNA cluster can be transcribed by Pol I and processed.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Karpen et al., 1988), our results show that individual ribosomal RNA units inserted in a heterologous genomic position outside of the native rDNA cluster can be transcribed by Pol I and processed (Figures 1C and 2C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that agrees with previous work, supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: Insertion of an individual rDNA unit in a euchromatic region in Drosophila was shown to be transcribed and to recruit nucleolar proteins to form nucleoli that are morphologically and functionally similar to endogenous nucleoli.
source: Insertion of an individual rDNA unit in a euchromatic region in Drosophila was shown to be transcribed and to recruit nucleolar proteins to form nucleoli that are morphologically and functionally similar to endogenous nucleoli (Karpen et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Karpen et al., 1988.

claim: Individual rDNA units in heterologous genomic locations are able to partially rescue the bobbed phenotype caused by decreased number of endogenous rDNA units.
source: Furthermore, individual rDNA units in heterologous genomic locations are able to partially rescue the bobbed phenotype caused by decreased number of endogenous rDNA units, indicating that transgenic rRNA is functional and incorporated into ribosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rDNA transgene functionality.

claim: Individual rDNA insertions into different genomic sites in S. cerevisiae were shown to be competent in assembly of the RNA Polymerase I complex and production of ribosomal RNA.
source: Similarly, individual rDNA insertions into different genomic sites in S. cerevisiae were shown to be competent in assembly of the RNA Polymerase I complex and production of ribosomal RNA (Oakes et al., 2006 ).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Oakes et al., 2006.

claim: The repeated structure and genomic location of rDNA loci are not required for their transcription.
source: Thus, our results corroborate previous studies that suggest that the repeated structure and genomic location of rDNA loci are not required for their transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the current study's results and previous work.

claim: rDNA units that are interrupted by insertion of R1 and R2 retrotransposons are selectively repressed.
source: Previous studies suggested that rDNA units that are interrupted by insertion of R1 and R2 retrotransposons, which integrate into specific sites in 28S rDNA in Drosophila are selectively repressed (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003; Jolly and Thomas, 1980; Kidd and Glover, 1981; Long et al., 1981; Long et al., 1981).

claim: Variable levels of repression were observed upon integration of a non-transposon sequence in 28S rDNA in a native rDNA cluster.
source: Variable levels of repression were also observed upon integration of a non-transposon sequence in 28S rDNA in a native rDNA cluster (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003.

claim: The molecular mechanism by which interrupted rDNA units are repressed and its link to silencing of intact rDNA remained poorly understood.
source: The molecular mechanism by which interrupted rDNA units are repressed and its link to silencing of intact rDNA remained poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Integration of a sequence other than transposons can induce rDNA repression.
source: Our results indicate that integration of a sequence other than transposons can induce rDNA repression.
evidence: This is concluded from the results showing CFP insertion causes repression.

claim: Extremely truncated R2 copies were shown to be actively expressed, indicating that rDNA with very short insertions can escape silencing.
source: Interestingly, extremely truncated R2 copies were shown to be actively expressed, indicating that rDNA with very short insertions can escape silencing (Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Eickbush and Eickbush, 2003.

claim: The length of CFP (720 bp) is sufficient to induce repression.
source: However, although the length of CFP (720 bp) is shorter than the full-length R1 and R2 transposons (5.4 and 3.6 kb, respectively), it is sufficient to induce repression.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results showing CFP insertion causes repression.

claim: Integrating a heterologous sequence into rDNA induced silencing in mammals.
source: Integrating a heterologous sequence into rDNA also induced silencing in mammals, which lack transposons that specifically integrate into rDNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rDNA regulation in mammals.

claim: Integration of the human growth hormone gene into rat ribosomal locus caused deletion of the ribosomal sequence and silencing of rDNA.
source: Integration of the human growth hormone gene into rat ribosomal locus caused deletion of the ribosomal sequence and silencing of rDNA (Henderson and Robins, 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Henderson and Robins, 1982.

claim: Repression of rDNA copies interrupted by insertions of heterologous sequences seems to be an evolutionary conserved process that prevents production of aberrant rRNA.
source: Thus, repression of rDNA copies interrupted by insertions of heterologous sequences seems to be an evolutionary conserved process that prevents production of aberrant rRNA, which might interfere with proper ribosome assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both flies and mammals.

claim: Intact rDNA units also undergo silencing, albeit less frequently than interrupted units.
source: Although intact transgenes are expressed in a larger fraction of cells than interrupted transgenes, they are still not expressed in all cells, indicating that intact rDNA units also undergo silencing, albeit less frequently than interrupted units.
evidence: This is concluded from the HCR-FISH data showing variable expression of intact transgenes.

claim: SUMO depletion lead to dramatic increase in the expression of R1 and R2 transposons, which integrate in native rDNA clusters.
source: In search of the molecular mechanism of rDNA repression we found that SUMO depletion lead to dramatic increase in the expression of R1 and R2 transposons, which integrate in native rDNA clusters (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data in Figure 3.

claim: Potent derepression of R1 and R2 was observed only upon SUMO depletion, but not in piRNA pathway mutants or upon depletion of E3 SUMO ligase Su(var)2–10.
source: Potent derepression of R1 and R2 was observed only upon SUMO depletion, but not in piRNA pathway mutants (Ninova et al., 2020a) or upon depletion of E3 SUMO ligase Su(var)2–10 (Ninova et al., 2020a) indicating that SUMO plays a special role in repression of rDNA-targeting transposons that is independent of the piRNA pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing effects of different knockdowns on R1 and R2 expression.

claim: SUMO plays a special role in repression of rDNA-targeting transposons that is independent of the piRNA pathway.
source: Potent derepression of R1 and R2 was observed only upon SUMO depletion, but not in piRNA pathway mutants (Ninova et al., 2020a) or upon depletion of E3 SUMO ligase Su(var)2–10 (Ninova et al., 2020a) indicating that SUMO plays a special role in repression of rDNA-targeting transposons that is independent of the piRNA pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the specific effect of SUMO depletion on R1 and R2.

claim: Depletion of SUMO also activates rDNA transgenes indicating that they are repressed by the same mechanism that silences native rDNA units.
source: Furthermore, depletion of SUMO also activates rDNA transgenes indicating that they are repressed by the same mechanism that silences native rDNA units (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is concluded from the similar effects of SUMO depletion on endogenous and transgenic rDNA.

claim: SUMO KD increased expression of intact transgenes and released their repression in individual cells.
source: SUMO KD increased expression of intact transgenes and released their repression in individual cells indicating that the same SUMO-dependent pathway is responsible for repression of both interrupted and intact rDNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HCR-FISH data in Figure 4.

claim: The same SUMO-dependent pathway is responsible for repression of both interrupted and intact rDNA.
source: SUMO KD increased expression of intact transgenes and released their repression in individual cells indicating that the same SUMO-dependent pathway is responsible for repression of both interrupted and intact rDNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the effects of SUMO depletion on both intact and interrupted rDNA.

claim: SUMO-dependent repression correlates with the levels of nascent pre-rRNA and decreased Pol I occupancy at rDNA promoters.
source: SUMO-dependent repression correlates with the levels of nascent pre-rRNA (Figure 4B–D) and decreased Pol I occupancy at rDNA promoters (Figure 2C) suggesting that repression acts at the level of transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the HCR-FISH and ChIP data.

claim: Repression acts at the level of transcription.
source: SUMO-dependent repression correlates with the levels of nascent pre-rRNA (Figure 4B–D) and decreased Pol I occupancy at rDNA promoters (Figure 2C) suggesting that repression acts at the level of transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between SUMO depletion, increased nascent RNA, and increased Pol I occupancy.

claim: In mammals repression of rDNA units correlates with the presence of CpG DNA methylation and repressive histone marks near the rDNA promoter.
source: In mammals repression of rDNA units was shown to correlate with the presence of CpG DNA methylation and repressive histone marks near the rDNA promoter (Bird et al., 1981; Coffman et al., 2005; Conconi et al., 1989; Dammann et al., 1993; Flavell et al., 1988; Earley et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006; Santoro and Grummt, 2001; Santoro et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The chromatin remodeling complexes NoRC and NuRD are involved in rDNA repression probably by altering accessibility of the rDNA promoter to chromatin repressors.
source: Furthermore, the chromatin remodeling complexes NoRC and NuRD were shown to be involved in rDNA repression probably by altering accessibility of the rDNA promoter to chromatin repressors such as DNA methyltransferases, histone methyltransferases and deacetylases (Santoro et al., 2002; Strohner et al., 2001; Xie et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Drosophila lack DNA methylation.
source: Unlike mammals Drosophila lack DNA methylation (Urieli-Shoval et al., 1982), so this mechanism plays no role in rDNA repression in flies.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DNA methylation plays no role in rDNA repression in flies.
source: Unlike mammals Drosophila lack DNA methylation (Urieli-Shoval et al., 1982), so this mechanism plays no role in rDNA repression in flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of DNA methylation in Drosophila.

claim: Native (but not transgenic) rDNA units are enriched in H3K9me3.
source: Our results indicate that native (but not transgenic) rDNA units are enriched in H3K9me3, a histone mark associated with repression of genes transcribed by Pol II.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP data in Figure 5.

claim: The level of H3K9me3 remained high on rDNA units upon SUMO depletion.
source: However, the level of H3K9me3 remained high on rDNA units upon SUMO depletion (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP data in Figure 5.

claim: rDNA transgenes inserted in heterologous genomic locus are repressed by SUMO-dependent mechanism though they have low level of H3K9me3 mark compared to endogenous rDNA.
source: Furthermore rDNA transgenes inserted in heterologous genomic locus are repressed by SUMO-dependent mechanism though they have low level of H3K9me3 mark compared to endogenous rDNA.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing H3K9me3 levels and expression of transgenic vs endogenous rDNA.

claim: H3K9 methylation might contribute to rDNA silencing along with other pathways.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that H3K9 methylation might contribute to rDNA silencing along with other pathways, however, it cannot be the only component of SUMO-dependent repression mechanism.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that H3K9me3 levels don't change upon SUMO depletion but Su(var)3-9 knockdown has mild effects.

claim: H3K9 methylation cannot be the only component of SUMO-dependent repression mechanism.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that H3K9 methylation might contribute to rDNA silencing along with other pathways, however, it cannot be the only component of SUMO-dependent repression mechanism.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of correlation between H3K9me3 levels and SUMO-dependent repression.

claim: Large number of nuclear proteins are SUMOylated.
source: Large number of nuclear proteins are SUMOylated and SUMO is required for many nuclear processes (Nacerddine et al., 2005; Zhao and Blobel, 2005) including different stages of ribosome maturation (Heun, 2007; Takahashi et al., 2008; Finkbeiner et al., 2011) and transcriptional repression of protein-coding genes (Gill, 2005; Verger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SUMO is required for many nuclear processes including different stages of ribosome maturation and transcriptional repression of protein-coding genes.
source: Large number of nuclear proteins are SUMOylated and SUMO is required for many nuclear processes (Nacerddine et al., 2005; Zhao and Blobel, 2005) including different stages of ribosome maturation (Heun, 2007; Takahashi et al., 2008; Finkbeiner et al., 2011) and transcriptional repression of protein-coding genes (Gill, 2005; Verger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Depletion of SUMO in female germline caused changes in gene expression.
source: In agreement with known role of SUMO in Pol II transcription, its depletion in female germline caused changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis in the current study.

claim: SUMO depletion caused statistically significant >2 fold up-regulation of ~4% (323) and down-regulation of ~1.5% (138) of the analyzed genes.
source: We observed statistically significant >2 fold up-regulation of ~4% (323) and down-regulation of ~1.5% (138) of the analyzed genes (qval <0.05, likelihood ratio test).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis in the current study.

claim: The vast majority of affected genes changed within 2–10 fold upon SUMO depletion.
source: However, the vast majority of affected genes changed within 2–10 fold, in stark contrast to dramatic ~1000 and~300 fold upregulation of R1 and R2 elements upon SUMO depletion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis in the current study.

claim: No significantly enriched GO terms associated with the up- and down- regulated gene sets upon SUMO KD were found related to nucleolar function and/or rRNA transcription.
source: We did not find any significantly enriched GO terms associated with the up- and down- regulated gene sets upon SUMO KD related to nucleolar function and/or rRNA transcription (BH-adjusted p-value cutoff 0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The only gene associated with the cellular component GO term 'nucleolus' among down-regulated genes was smt3 itself.
source: Manual inspection showed that the only gene associated with the cellular component GO term 'nucleolus' ('GO:0005730') and offspring terms among down-regulated genes was smt3 itself.
evidence: This is a finding from manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claim: Only two out of the 323 up-regulated genes - ph-p and CG9123 - are associated with the 'nucleolus' GO term.
source: Only two out of the 323 up-regulated genes - ph-p and CG9123 - are associated with the 'nucleolus' GO term, however, neither of them has known function in rDNA expression.
evidence: This is a finding from manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claim: There is no direct indication that expression of genes involved in rDNA transcription and nucleolar function is affected by SUMO depletion.
source: Therefore, while we cannot completely exclude a possibility of secondary effects of SUMO depletion, there is no direct indication that expression of genes involved in rDNA transcription and nucleolar function is affected by SUMO depletion.
evidence: This is concluded from the GO enrichment and manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claim: SUMO plays direct role in rDNA silencing through modification of one or several proteins involved in rDNA expression.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that SUMO plays direct role in rDNA silencing through modification of one or several proteins involved in rDNA expression.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: Many nucleolar proteins, including several components of RNA pol I machinery and Udd protein, are SUMOylated in vivo.
source: Second, our analysis of SUMOylated proteome using both targeted and unbiased approaches indicates that many nucleolar proteins, including several components of RNA pol I machinery and Udd protein previously implicated in rDNA expression (Zhang et al., 2014), are SUMOylated in vivo (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from SUMOylation assays and proteomic analysis.

claim: Recruitment of SUMO ligase Ubc9 to rDNA transgene led to its repression revealing direct effect of local SUMOylation on rDNA expression.
source: Third, recruitment of SUMO ligase Ubc9 to rDNA transgene led to its repression revealing direct effect of local SUMOylation on rDNA expression (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the tethering experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Local SUMOylation in proximity of gene promoters was shown to induce repression of Pol II driven transcription in Drosophila and mammals.
source: Finally, local SUMOylation in proximity of gene promoters was shown to induce repression of Pol II driven transcription in Drosophila and mammals (Ninova et al., 2020a; Ninova et al., 2020b; Stielow et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2011; Lehembre et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2003; Yang and Sharrocks, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SUMOylation at promoters is required for repression induced by KRAB-ZFPs, the largest family of mammalian transcriptional silencers.
source: Particularly, SUMOylation at promoters is required for repression induced by KRAB-ZFPs, the largest family of mammalian transcriptional silencers (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Pol I-driven rRNA promoters were found to be one of the most prominent sites of active sumoylation in human cells.
source: Pol I-driven rRNA promoters were found to be one of the most prominent sites of active sumoylation in human cells (Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibition of sumoylation caused upregulation of rRNA expression in human cells.
source: Remarkably, inhibition of sumoylation caused upregulation of rRNA expression indicating that the role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals (Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals.
source: Remarkably, inhibition of sumoylation caused upregulation of rRNA expression indicating that the role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals (Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both Drosophila and human cells.

claim: SUMOylation of chromatin-associated proteins might act as a molecular mark for rDNA repression.
source: Our results suggest that SUMOylation of chromatin-associated proteins might act as a molecular mark for rDNA repression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Repression might require modification of several chromatin-bound proteins rather than one specific target.
source: However, modest R1/R2 upregulation observed upon depletion of several proteins suggest that repression might require modification of several chromatin-bound proteins rather than one specific target.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi screen results showing modest effects of individual protein knockdowns.

claim: Promiscuous modification of multiple proteins is in line with the findings that SUMOylation consensus is very simple and quite common in the fly proteome.
source: Promiscuous modification of multiple proteins is in line with the findings that SUMOylation consensus is very simple and quite common in the fly proteome (Nie et al., 2009) and our results that show that multiple nucleolar proteins are SUMOylated.
evidence: This is inferred from the computational analysis and SUMOylation assays.

claim: The proposal that rDNA repression depend on cumulative SUMOylation of several proteins localized on rDNA is corroborated by studies in yeast that led to the ''SUMO spray'' hypothesis.
source: The proposal that rDNA repression depend on cumulative SUMOylation of several proteins localized on rDNA corroborated by studies in yeast that led to the ''SUMO spray'' hypothesis (Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012) which suggests that SUMOylation of multiple proteins localized in physical proximity is required to induce downstream response in SUMO-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to studies in yeast.

claim: SUMOylation of multiple proteins localized in physical proximity is required to induce downstream response in SUMO-dependent pathway according to the SUMO spray hypothesis.
source: The proposal that rDNA repression depend on cumulative SUMOylation of several proteins localized on rDNA corroborated by studies in yeast that led to the ''SUMO spray'' hypothesis (Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012) which suggests that SUMOylation of multiple proteins localized in physical proximity is required to induce downstream response in SUMO-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is the SUMO spray hypothesis from yeast studies, supported by citation.

claim: Multiple interactions between SUMOylated proteins and proteins that bind SUMO act synergistically.
source: Importantly, multiple interactions between SUMOylated proteins and proteins that bind SUMO act synergistically and thus SUMOylation of any single protein is neither necessary nor sufficient to trigger downstream processes (Jentsch and Psakhye, 2013; Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO spray mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: SUMOylation of any single protein is neither necessary nor sufficient to trigger downstream processes in SUMO spray mechanism.
source: Importantly, multiple interactions between SUMOylated proteins and proteins that bind SUMO act synergistically and thus SUMOylation of any single protein is neither necessary nor sufficient to trigger downstream processes (Jentsch and Psakhye, 2013; Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO spray mechanism, supported by citations.
